The Annular seabream, Diplodus annularis, is a commercially important sparid species inhabiting shallow coastal waters of the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs following a brief incubation period. Based on observations of the congener Diplodus puntazzo, egg hatching under controlled conditions occurs after approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], defining the age at birth for this species. The yolk-sac larva, initially lecithotrophic, possesses an extremely small wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of related sparids. This negligible initial mass underscores the vulnerability of the planktonic larval phase, during which individuals must rapidly acquire exogenous feeding capabilities to survive.

As the free-swimming larva develops, it undergoes a dramatic increase in somatic mass before reaching sexual maturation. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis reveal that the ultimate wet weight attained by an adult Diplodus annularis is approximately 330 grams [Wwi = approximately 330 grams]. This asymptotic mass represents the maximum body size reached after several years of sustained feeding, with most individuals achieving this weight by the time they transition to the demersal adult habitat. The capacity to attain this adult body mass appears strongly linked to food availability in coastal seagrass meadows, where the species actively forages for crustaceans and molluscs. Comparative data with other Mediterranean sparids, such as Diplodus vulgaris, indicate that a 330 gram maximum is relatively modest, consistent with the species' smaller ultimate body length.

The species exhibits a moderate life span typical of small-bodied sparids inhabiting temperate seas. Mark-recapture studies in the Gulf of Lion, conducted at a mean annual water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], have documented that the maximum lifespan for Diplodus annularis is 2555 days [am = 2555 days], equivalent to seven full years. This longevity, measured from the date of hatching to natural mortality, reflects a life-history strategy that includes an extended juvenile phase before reproductive investment begins. The 19 °C thermal regime characteristic of this region appears to optimize metabolic efficiency, allowing individuals to sustain both somatic growth and gonadal development without accelerated aging. At higher temperatures, metabolic acceleration might shorten this achievable lifespan.

Reproductive activity in Diplodus annularis commences once individuals attain a specific body length indicative of gonadal maturation. A comprehensive analysis of specimens collected across the Mediterranean established that the total length at puberty is 11.2 centimeters [Lp = 11.2 centimeters]. At this size, the onset of gametogenesis is triggered, marking the transition from the immature juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase. Consequently, the species' spawning season is protracted, extending from spring through early autumn. In the warm, stable thermal conditions of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] prevalent during this period in the Adriatic Sea, females achieve their maximum reproduction rate by producing approximately 581 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 581 eggs per spawning event] with multiple spawning events occurring across the season [F_R_i = multiple spawning events occurring across the season].

The ultimate total length recorded for the species in the wild provides a key measure of its maximum somatic size. The largest authenticated specimen of Diplodus annularis measured 27.5 centimeters [Li = 27.5 centimeters] in total length, a value that sets the upper boundary for growth within natural populations. This maximum recorded length is attained through a combination of rapid juvenile growth and a slower, asymptotic adult phase, with the most significant increases occurring during the first three years of life before the growth curve plateaus. Understanding this size limit is essential for establishing effective minimum landing sizes in fisheries management and conservation planning for this commercially harvested sparid across its Mediterranean range.
